speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Innovation is crucial for our nation's continued economic growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It allows our enterprises to create new products and services, and gives them a competitive edge over their rivals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Enterprises need to be able to effectively protect and commercialise their intellectual property (IP) to preserve their competitive edge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Committee on the Future Economy recognised this when it stated that a strong IP ecosystem is needed to support innovation and technology adoption.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Patents (Amendment) Bill introduces several improvements to our patent system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These amendments allow our patent system to better support innovators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To provide some background, let me briefly describe IPOS' patent search and examination process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Before a patent is granted for an invention, it must be "new" and "inventive".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: An IPOS examiner searches publicly available information at the time of the patent application to understand the current state of technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is known as the "state of the art".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The examiner then examines the invention in the patent application against the "state of the art" to determine whether the invention is, indeed, new and inventive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is the standard practice for all patent offices around the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Under this system, if an inventor publicly discloses his invention before applying for a patent, this information will form part of the "state of the art".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, when he subsequently applies for a patent, the invention may not be assessed to be new or inventive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Patents Act contains a "grace period provision" that allows for limited circumstances under which the disclosure of an invention will not be considered part of the "state of the art".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, if the invention is disclosed at one of the international exhibitions on a limited list, or is disclosed in the publication of a learned society, it will not be included in the "state of the art" if the application is filed within 12 months of the disclosure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This grace period provision encourages knowledge sharing and promotes learning while preserving the inventor's commercial interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Clause 2 of the Patents (Amendment) Bill expands the situations covered by the grace period provision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Clause 2(b) will allow any disclosure of the invention originating from the inventor to be covered by the grace period provision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In other words, the grace period provision will not be limited to disclosures at specific international exhibitions or in a learned society publication.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This broadening of the grace period provision is in line with practices in the United States (US), Australia, Japan and Korea.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It updates our legislation so that our patents regime can be more consistent with modern realities and practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Advances in communication technology have connected people across the globe in ways not previously envisaged, and disclosures of technology occur in many situations not contemplated by the current Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, inventors may need to reveal the invention to potential investors, or share it online to reach out to a larger community of experts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It should be emphasised that disclosing an invention before applying for a patent still carries risks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Not all jurisdictions have a similarly broad grace period provision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We would, therefore, strongly encourage inventors to always be judicious about disclosing their inventions before applying for a patent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: IPOS will work with stakeholders and IP professionals to ensure that this message is conveyed clearly to patent applicants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I now turn to the amendments in clause 3 of the present Bill relating to the closure of the foreign route to obtaining a patent in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is another step in our quest to improve the quality of patents granted in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In 2013, IPOS' in-house patent examination unit commenced operations, marking the first time Singapore had the capabilities to examine our patent applications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In February 2014, we tightened our patent system to only allow a patent to be granted if it meets the patentability requirements in our law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This will increase the quality of our granted patents and marks the further maturation of our patent system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Patent applications undergo search and examination before a patent is granted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There are currently three search and examination routes in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, under the "local route", the full search and examination are conducted by IPOS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, under the "mixed route", applicants submit the search report issued by the foreign patent office for the same invention, and IPOS conducts only the examination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Third, under the "foreign route", applicants submit the full search and examination report issued by a foreign patent office for the same invention, and IPOS conducts only a limited-scope Supplementary Examination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The limited-scope Supplementary Examination does not cover the same grounds as a full examination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In particular, the invention is not assessed on the key requirements of being new and inventive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Thus, patents may be granted under the foreign route for inventions that would not have met the standards for patentability under the local or mixed route.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is because these foreign route patents were assessed to be new and inventive by a foreign patent office, whose standards may differ from Singapore's.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: IPOS has been actively engaging the patent profession on the closure of the foreign route.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With this change, local patent agents and IP lawyers will adjust their practice to take on higher value work as all the patent applications they handle will have to undergo full examination by IPOS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Patents (Amendment) Bill will also implement procedural improvements to the application process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Clause 3(c) will allow patent applications greater flexibility in switching between search and examination routes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This will make our patent application process more applicant-friendly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Clause 3(d) will allow IPOS to treat an application as abandoned if the applicant does not, after receiving a search report, request for an examination report within the prescribed timeframe.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It will also facilitate the release of new ideas and technologies for the public's use if the patent applicant is no longer interested in obtaining protection.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill implements a number of improvements to the patent application process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is part of our efforts to better support the national innovation agenda by helping companies protect and sharpen their competitive edge, grow and create good jobs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is our duty to ensure the IP surrounding these are firmly protected on our shores.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The law on patents is a key jigsaw piece in the protection of these intellectual rights.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I, therefore, rise in support of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore has come a long way in its IP laws.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From our early years as a nation, Singapore has strengthened our laws, such that they support our changing economy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Information, innovation and proprietary rights are key aspects of our present and future economy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, the safe protection of IP is crucial.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They allow innovations to be protected, and I should declare here my interest as a litigator whose practice includes, in part, IP litigation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In terms of filing patents, Singapore has entered into important international treaties to establish and advance Singapore's status as an IP hub, such as the TRIPS Agreement, or the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore's strong laws protect and promote innovation and have attracted parties from other countries to register with us.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since our early years, we have moved from re-registration of United Kingdom (UK) Patents to outsourcing the search and examination process to operationalising our very own office, IPOS International, to handle the search and examination process.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Patent Prosecution Highway allows fast and efficient search processes by collaboration with other countries, such as Japan, US, Australia, Germany, UK, Korea, China and Mexico.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, Singapore's search and examination reports may be delivered within 60 to 90 days.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore is also the first Supplementary International Search Authority to carry out searches in Chinese.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, IPOS International has become recognised by the World Intellectual Property Organisation as an International Searching Authority and International Preliminary Examining Authority (ISA/IPEA).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These important and foundational steps were key to the promotion of Singapore as a safe and predictable IP hub based on the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This second, all ­foreign, route is based on the reliance on the final results of the search and examination report of a corresponding application, corresponding international application, or related national phase application.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It works on the presumption that the reports are reliable and accurate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But to ensure the quality of patents, it is better, if not much better, if we conduct the substantive evaluation ourselves.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having said this, we should not underestimate the load.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead, we should approach the task with a large amount of preparation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On this related issue, could the Minister kindly elaborate on what has been done to ensure that even with the closure of the foreign route, Singapore will continue to be an attractive place, and an attractive financial place, to file patents?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister also confirm that we have reliable resources to meet any demand at cost-effective prices?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This allows the inventor to disclose information without jeopardising his patent application.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a result, inventors may very well be able to attract investors or publish scientific papers without needing to wait for a patent.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Keeping abreast with the shifts in our economy is important, especially the protection of IP.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, this cannot be done without a reliable regulatory framework in the form of IP laws.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It will further consolidate Singapore's position as an IP hub and, Mdm Speaker, I therefore support it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, it is entirely plausible for a would-be inventor to disclose details of his invention in reasonable circumstances outside the narrow exceptions listed in section 14(4) to (7).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Previous case law has set a high standard that novelty would be ruined as long as even one member of the public has unrestricted use of the information.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is problematic, especially where would-be inventors, in their excitement or by slip of tongue, informally discuss details of the invention with family members or close friends.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The heavy penalty of unpatentability and the wastage of months or years of working worth large sums of money is unfair, and the law should be flexible enough to allow for such minor disclosures to be excused.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the two narrow exceptions for prior disclosure, namely, display at an international exhibition or by description in a paper read before a learned society, are unduly restrictive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is conceivable that would-be inventors make disclosures that are entirely reasonable for their professions, especially in the scientific fields.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, scientists often give journalistic interviews or write scientific journals on laboratory breakthroughs that they have discovered, even before commercialisation of a product from the said discovery.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such disclosures are commonplace in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) academia, where articles in prestigious journals could determine the standing of a scientist in his community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To have no invention patentable from such a disclosure would unfairly impose a period of silence on the scientist, who may only publicly disclose his breakthrough until after the date of patent filing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I wish to raise just one point for clarification.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 14(4)(e) refers to "disclosure of matter constituting an invention to the public" while existing sections 14(4)(a) to (d) merely refer to "disclosure".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to more local innovators taking advantage of and flourishing under our robust IP protection regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr de Souza asked about initiatives to ensure that Singapore remains an attractive place to file patents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, there are the various Patent Prosecution Highways (PPHs) that Mr de Souza mentioned.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These arrangements cover important markets like China, the US, Europe, Japan, Korea and Australia.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: IPOS is also part of a similar arrangement in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), known as the ASEAN Patent Examination Co-operation (ASPEC) programme.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All in, the PPHs and ASPEC cover more than 30 jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: IPOS also has an agreement with Cambodia to allow the re-registration of a Singapore patent in Cambodia.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hence, with a Singapore granted patent, a business can access a combined market of over 20 million people.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In February, IPOS also announced reductions in its patent search and examination fees.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A further discount will be given when the applicant chooses to rely on the search report or preliminary examination report issued by IPOS as an ISA and IPEA under the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All these connections to larger markets outside Singapore are aimed at making Singapore an attractive place to file patents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition, we are also positioning Singapore to capture patent work, even when applicants are looking to file patents in other jurisdictions and not in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Being a PCT International Searching and Preliminary Examining Authority, IPOS is able to provide search and examination services to applicants who file in other jurisdictions via PCT.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Besides Singapore, IPOS can do this PCT examination work for applicants from the US, Japan, Mexico, Indonesia, Vietnam and Cambodia.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Further, given the large Chinese market, IPOS' ability to search Chinese patent documents can be an additional attraction for these PCT applicants.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Through these measures, IPOS hopes to attract patent work to Singapore, even in cases where an applicant might decide not to file in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will create more work for IP professionals, such as patent agents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr de Souza also asked whether we are adequately resourced to handle the increased workload from applicants switching to the local mixed routes: yes, we are.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, the Ministry of Law and IPOS will continue to ensure that there is a sufficient pipeline of skilled IP manpower to provide patent agent services.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Graduates from the patent agent specialisation track of this programme can go on to take the Patent Agents Qualifying Examinations to become patent agents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The unit will be able to handle the anticipated increase in work.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: From PCT statistics, IPOS is the top, out of 21 international authorities, in terms of timeliness to issue International Search Reports.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng had a point for clarification regarding the new section 14(4)(e) inserted by clause 2(b) of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Sections 14(4)(a) to (e) each describes different circumstances of disclosure to the public that are to be disregarded during the determination of the "state of the art" which the examiner considers in assessing whether the invention is "new" and "inventive".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Section 14(4)(e) is intended to extend the circumstances of disclosure that are to be disregarded beyond those stated in the current section 14(4)(a) to 14(4)(d).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For all the grounds in section 14(4)(a) to (e), disclosure even to one person not under the obligation of confidentiality constitutes disclosure to the public.
